title: Technical Development
text: Component: TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The Technology Development component describes software development for Xenbase. This includes code in the database, web applications, data scheme, user and curator interfaces, and innovative data visualizations. New data types and curation efforts require new systems, tools and software interfaces to be built. Interfaces must be designed to allow our community members to browse and interrogate the data via our web portal. This renewal will add additional content requiring new technology development, including deeper GO support, single-cell omics, new types of NGS sequencing, variant analyses, and more extensive human disease and phenotype analysis tools and the development of machine learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to accelerate curation, genomic analysis and for users to query Xenbase content. Aim 1 Maintain and improve Xenbase functionality Aim 2 Support expanded and novel content – GO, single cell, sequence variants & disease modeling Aim 3 Developing AI/ML-assisted curation and content.

title: Nuclear Control of Cell Growth and Differentiation (NC)
text: NUCLEAR CONTROL OF CELL GROWTH AND DIFFERENTIATION PROGRAM ABSTRACT The Nuclear Control of Cell Growth and Differentiation (NC) Program is a basic science program that provides innovative approaches that lead to impactful understanding of the mechanistic basis of cancer development. The leadership, membership, and activities combine to achieve a particular aspect of the Huntsman Cancer Institute (HCI) mission statement—“to understand cancer from its beginnings.” This is accomplished through experimentation focused on mechanisms underlying basic nuclear processes and pathways that go awry in cancer cells and contribute to oncogenesis. NC members use innovative discovery science and preclinical models for the purpose of dissecting fundamental aspects of cell growth and differentiation that occur in and/or impact the nucleus. Within these broad goals, research in the NC Program pursues three Specific Aims: 1) to decipher the roles of gene dysregulation in cancer; 2) to define relationships between metabolic dysregulation and gene networks in cancer; and 3) to reveal altered mechanisms of DNA damage, replication, and repair in cancer. Each of these three Specific Aims involves the investigation of both normal nuclear processes, as well as their dysregulation in cancer. A deep and fundamental understanding of both states is needed to develop the most effective diagnostics, the best tailored therapies, and the clearest and most effective guidelines related to prevention—in alignment with the mission of HCI. The NC Program has 33 members with academic appointments in 12 University of Utah departments in three schools/colleges. Program members are well funded, with a strongly positive funding trajectory that is increasingly cancer-focused. Peer-reviewed funding totals $11.1M in direct costs, of which $3.9M (35%) derives from the National Cancer Institute. Program members published 329 peer-reviewed papers; 12% represented intra-programmatic efforts and 27% resulted from inter-programmatic collaborations. Twenty- seven percent of publications were in journals with an impact factor greater than 10. As a cancer-focused basic science program, the NC Program has a major positive impact on the Cancer Center through innovation and research excellence in gene regulation, cancer metabolism, and genome stability—as well as enhancing education and training of HCI trainees in these areas. Thus, NC provides discovery science that can be translated to the clinic and population, with special attention to understanding basic mechanisms underlying cancers of high incidence in HCI’s catchment area, including melanoma, lung, breast, and childhood cancers. NC Program members continue to play leading roles in cancer-focused discovery research and partner with colleagues in all four HCI Research Programs for translational impact.

title: Biomarker, Biospecimen, and Genetics Core
text: Project Summary – Biomarker, Biospecimens, and Genetics Core (BBGC) The Indiana Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (IADRC) has a strong history of innovative research in fluid and imaging biomarkers and neuroimaging genetics Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research and will continue to focus on the role of biomarkers and genetics as predictors of clinical trajectories and risk for adverse events in response to treatment among the broader group of individuals with early- and late-onset AD and related dementias (ADRD), as well as those in preclinical and prodromal stages such as mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The BBGC plays a central role in this overall focus through the collection of uniform biospecimens and supporting and conducting research on fluid biomarkers and genetics. It also supports multiple national efforts through the broad sharing of specimens and data. The BBGC leverages the unique patient populations and genomic and biomarker-related resources at Indiana University School of Medicine to support each Core as well as the overall goals of the IADRC. The BBGC fosters new research directions through the common banking of samples from a broad range of research groups, responsive to IUSM investigator-driven and national research initiatives. These samples are then available to address research questions that are central to the interests of the IADRC. In addition, these samples are available for collaborative studies, thereby enhancing the power of all ADRC studies focused on disease susceptibility, onset, and progression. In this application, the BBGC will expand its scope by incorporating new directions in fluid biomarker development. The BBGC will leverage the extensive experience of new Core lead Dr. Donna Wilcock, as well as continuing Co-Investigator Dr. Jeff Dage, both of whom are internationally recognized experts in fluid biomarker research and development, with the goal to assess novel plasma and CSF biomarkers of ADRD to improve risk assessment, diagnosis, and patient stratification for clinical trials. The IADRC BBGC proposes the following specific aims: 1) Obtain longitudinal biospecimen samples from all participants seen in the Clinical Core and support local and national research studies. 2) Obtain AD and ADRD biomarker data to support ongoing studies of cognitive impairment and dementia. 3) Obtain and analyze genetic data for center participants to support ongoing studies of cognitive impairment and dementia. 4) Provide education on the development, validation and design of biomarker studies and facilitate cross- core collaboration.

title: Washington University Center for Cellular Imaging
text: WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY CENTER FOR CELLULAR IMAGING (WUCCI) SHARED RESOURCE: PROJECT SUMMARY Elucidating the mechanisms involved in the development and progression of cancer requires a deep understanding of how changes in tissue / cellular structure relate to loss of function. Imaging technologies have evolved rapidly over the last decade, generating vast improvements in resolution, sensitivity, and speed, and creating fundamentally new opportunities for studying biological processes across many orders of magnitude in real-time in living cells and organisms. The Washington University Center for Cellular Imaging (WUCCI) provides (i) reliable and affordable access to cutting-edge light and electron microscopy instrumentation, (ii) expert guidance in imaging assay design, specimen preparation, image acquisition and analysis, (iii) educational opportunities in the form of hands-on trainings, lunch and learn lectures, workshops and a monthly journal club and (iv) novel imaging and analysis methodologies. As a new Cancer Center Support Grant (CCSG) shared resource (SR), WUCCI will provide an integrated approach to investigate the structure and dynamic behavior of cells and tissues in cancer-related studies. By leveraging a significant institutional investment, SCC researchers gain instant access to a wide variety of advanced cellular microscopy tools which will serve to accelerate the pace, expand the scope, and improve the efficiency of their research. WUCCI services meet the unique requirements of numerous investigators over a wide range of basic and translational research, as well as attract new investigators into the cancer research arena. Importantly, users benefit from the in-depth technical expertise of the Director (James Fitzpatrick) and technical staff with regard to experimental design and interpretation of data. Over the past three years, WUCCI has worked with multiple SCC researchers to implement new imaging assays. These have included the application of two-photon intravital microscopy to longitudinally track disseminated tumor cells in a mouse model of dormancy (Sheila Stewart [MCBP]), the development of x-ray contrast agents to delineate metastatic tumor boundaries in murine long bones (Katherine Weilbeacher [BCRP]), and the application of focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) serial block face imaging to acquire three-dimensional volumes of mouse gastric tissue at the nanoscale (Jason Mills [MCBP]). In 2018, WUCCI served 235 research laboratories, 75 of which were SCC investigators whose usage represented ~20% of the overall SR consumption. Future plans for the next project period include the acquisition of a light-sheet fluorescence microscope recently funded by the NIH S10 program for the high-speed volumetric imaging of living organoids and cleared tissues, as well as the implementation of the Visiopharm Oncotopix IHC and ISH image analysis platform. We anticipate that requests for WUCCI services will continue to grow given the need for advanced microscopic imaging and analysis in the study of cancer. Thus, WUCCI, as a new CCSG shared resource, will provide essential services to SCC investigators throughout the next project period.

title: Mechanisms of voltage regulation of membrane transport
text:
SLC9 family of membrane transporters play key roles in pH and salt homeostasis in all living cells
and genetic mutations in these proteins have been linked to a variety of pathological conditions
such as epilepsies, autism, digestive disorders, male infertility, etc. In this proposal we will
determine high resolution structures and investigate functional mechanisms of a unique SLC9
family member, SLC9C1. This will advance our understanding of how this protein is regulated by
physical and chemical stimuli and guide developments of new intervention strategies to treat
pathophysiological conditions arising from disfunction of these proteins.

title: The roles of microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase-1 in regulating neuronal development
text:
The proposed research project is relevant to public health because it proposes to identify the cellular and
molecular mechanisms disrupted in neurodevelopmental disorders. It will advance our understanding of disease
etiology and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for patients.

title: Immunology of Post-Treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome
text:
Project 2, Immunology of Post-treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome
The human immune response plays an important role in protecting us from disease but can also cause disease
when not responding properly. In this Project, we will use new technologies to identify how immune responses
may differ between people who recover from Lyme disease versus those who have persistent symptoms.
Understanding the differences may lead us to new diagnostics and strategies for treating people with persistent
symptoms after treatment.

title: High Speed 1000 fps Angiography for X-ray Image Guided Cardiovascular Interventions
text:
Project Narrative / Public Health Relevance
Our project is dedicated to enhancing patient care by developing a high-speed x-ray camera system designed
to accurately image blood flow in the arteries during x-ray image-guided interventional procedures for diagnosis
and treatment of vascular diseases such as coronary artery disease, brain aneurysms, and others.

title: Discovery of small molecule inhibitors for protein N-terminal acetyltransferase D
text:
There are no small molecule inhibitors in existence to target NatD. This application is the first
study that seeks to discover novel small molecules targeting NatD. The proposed research is
relevant to public health because the developed NatD inhibitors will increase our understanding
of how NatD contributes to cancer progression and its value as a therapeutic target, which is
relevant to the mission of NCI.

title: Suicide Prevention in Cancer Survivorship: A Mixed-Methods Study of Veteran Cancer Survivors
text:
Veterans are at increased risk for cancer, which can have lasting physical and psychological effects. Studies in
the general population indicate that cancer survivors are at higher risk for suicidal ideation, suicide attempt,
and suicide. Suicidal thoughts and behaviors among cancer survivors may be associated with the physical
effects of cancer and its treatment, such as chronic pain and impaired functioning, as well as psychological
effects, including depression and anxiety. Few studies have examined risk for and the experience of suicidal
thoughts and behaviors among Veterans with a history of cancer despite an increased risk for mental health
problems and suicide within the Veteran population. To address this knowledge gap, this study aims to provide
a holistic picture of suicidal ideation and suicide attempts among a national sample of Veteran cancer survivors
who have recently completed treatment. Study findings will inform the development of suicide prevention
strategies in cancer survivorship settings and future research to implement and evaluate such programs.

title: Privacy-Aware Federated Learning for Breast Cancer Risk Assessment
text: Successful completion of this proposal will lead to a trustworthy zero-code federated learning (FL) software framework, lowering the barrier to leverage data from all populations in large-scale, secure, de- centralized multi-institutional collaborations, without the need to share patient data, thereby i) overcoming legal, privacy, and data-ownership concerns, and ii) paving the way to accelerating discovery in healthcare. This framework will further support the clinical impact and lifecycle of FL studies by offering a) pre-trained breast cancer risk assessment models leveraging multi-site data of women undergoing breast screening across 5 U.S. states, and functionality specific to b) improving these pre-trained models, by including additional geographically distinct sites, c) data synthesis for data augmentation & privacy preservation, based on realistic synthetic data matching each site’s local patient population characteristics, and d) an automated mechanism for quantitative & interpretable determination of optimal privacy preservation.

title: Epigenetic regulatory function of Bap1 in dentate gyrus development
text:
Neurodevelopmental disorders affect a growing population of patients worldwide and epigenetic changes are
highly implicated in these conditions. This proposal aims to understand the role and mechanism underlying
epigenetic regulation in the development of the dentate gyrus, a crucial structure for learning and memory. Our
study will contribute to an important basis for understanding the physiological mechanisms, diagnosis, and
treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Statistical Methods for Inferring Gene-Phenotype Associations Using Omic Data from Gene Knockout and Human Phenotype Studies
text:
MorPhiC consortium will deliver rich resources of molecular and cellular phenotypes before and after gene
knockout using in vitro cellular systems. We will develop statistical methods to combine MorPhiC resources and
omic data in human phenotype studies to infer gene functions in diverse settings and identify potential causal
genes of human phenotypes. Our methods pave the way to use MorPhiC resources to study the impact of gene
loss on complex phenotypes.

title: PROJECT 3 - Kynurenine-AhR Signaling Effects on Mitophagy and Senescence with Age in Bone Marrow Stem Cells
text:
In the current application, we will test our hypothesis that inhibition of KYN-AhR signaling in bone
and bone marrow stromal cells can effectively prevent or reduce age-dependent bone loss.
Furthermore, we will determine the molecular mechanisms by which KYN-AhR signaling
modulates mitophagy/autophagy and premature senescence in bone marrow stromal cells and
bone cells.

title: Transformative microscopes to image across spatiotemporal scales
text:
My proposed research program will provide technologies to extend the reach of optical
microscopy, from subcellular dynamics up to entire model organisms. At the same time,
we will bridge these different scales through smart microscopy, which autonomously
adjusts temporal and spatial resolution to efficiently (in terms of time, amount of data
and sample irradiation) explore a specimen. If successful, these technologies may
prove transformative in biological and biomedical research.

title: Engineering Reconstituted Ovaries with Developmentally Matched In Vitro-derived Germ Cells to Improve Outcomes of In Vitro Oogenesis
text:
The reconstituted ovary (rOvary) provides a platform to generate stem cell-derived oocytes from stem cells,
offering a promising solution to infertility, but most oocytes produced in the system do not support embryonic
development. I have identified stark differences in germline differentiation between immature stem cell-derived
germ cells (PGCLCs) and developmentally older germ cells found within the rOvary, with PGCs entering
meiosis earlier, forming follicles at the appropriate time, and generating significantly larger oocytes. Using
methods to mature PGCLCs before introduction to the rOvary, I propose to improve the health of oocytes
generated by this platform through better matching germ cell and somatic cell developmental timing.

title: Bioinformatics Omic Platform for Circadian Biomedical Research
text:
Circadian rhythms are fundamental for biology and medicine. Modern high-throughput technologies are
revealing how the concentrations of many molecular species, including transcripts, proteins, and metabolites
oscillate with the day and night cycle in every species, tissues, and organs. In close collaboration with life
scientists, this project will develop the informatics tools that will enable the collection, integration, and analyses
of this wealth of information and lead to novel and fundamental insights about the organization and regulation
of circadian oscillations, their roles in health and disease, and their future applications to precision medicine.

title: Clinical and Physiological Determinants of Pregnancy-Related Cardiovascular Complications
text:
The United States is facing a maternal health crisis and pregnancies that are complicated
by heart disease are at highest risk for maternal death. This research will apply innovative
tools including data science, machine learning, and vascular physiology testing to identify
clinical and physiological determinants of cardiovascular complications during pregnancy
and develop new tools to capture pregnant women at high risk for pregnancy-related
cardiovascular complications. Our work may lead to integration of data science and
machine learning tools into routine pregnancy care to reduce cardiovascular complications
and improve maternal outcomes.

title: Distinct roles of chromatin regulation in transcriptome and genome maintenance in corticogenesis
text:
Genomic DNA is packaged into a compact form around chromatin, which is a highly organized complex of DNA
and proteins that needs to be reorganized by chromatin remodelers to enable biological processes such as gene
expression, DNA replication, and DNA damage repair. Recent human genetic findings have indicated that
mutations in genes encoding chromatin remodelers are an important contribution to disorders of brain
development, including autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability. In this study, we seek to understand
the distinct functions of chromatin remodeling in gene expression and DNA damage and repair, and the
consequences of their disruption on the development of the brain.

title: Genome editing therapeutics for the treatment of aortic aneurysm in Marfan Syndrome
text:
Marfan syndrome is the most common hereditary connective tissue disorder with a prevalence of 1:5,000-
1:10,000, and despite pharmacologic therapy to limit aortic aneurysm, many affected individuals will require
aortic root surgery and remain at risk of life-threatening aortic dissection. This work aims to develop genome
editing strategies for the treatment of aortic aneurysm in Marfan syndrome. These technologies could form the
basis of cures for Marfan syndrome as well as other currently untreatable genetic conditions.
